Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Ecological and Individual-Level Factors Associated With Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome Notifications and in-Hospital Mortality Among Hospitalized Patients in Chile, 2005-2022.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a severe zoonotic disease caused by Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus, ANDV), with significant public health burden in Chile. Despite decades of surveillance, knowledge gaps remain regarding the ecological drivers of notification burden and the individual-level determinants of in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients. This study aimed to address both dimensions simultaneously, providing a multilevel characterization of HCPS epidemiology in Chile from 2005 to 2022. METHODS: Two complementary analyses were conducted. First, an ecological study examined district-level HCPS notifications (2005-2022) using a negative binomial mixed-effects model, with predictors including male population rate, urbanization proportion, population density, season and burned area due to forest fires during the most recent summer season. Second, an individual-level analysis of hospitalized HCPS patients (2010-2020) used a logistic mixed-effects model to identify correlates of in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients, including age, sex, indigenous group affiliation, hospitalization duration and number of surgical interventions. RESULTS: A total of 886 HCPS cases were notified across 187 districts, averaging 49.2 cases per year. Notifications were positively associated with higher male population rates and greater burned area due to forest fires, and negatively associated with urbanization and population density. Among 462 hospitalized patients, the in-hospital case-fatality ratio was 19.7%. Older age, female sex and indigenous group affiliation were significantly associated with higher in-hospital mortality risk among hospitalized patients. Shorter hospitalization duration and greater number of surgical interventions, as correlates of clinical severity and complexity, were also associated with in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients. CONCLUSIONS: HCPS notification burden in Chile is shaped by environmental and demographic factors, with forest fire activity representing a novel and actionable ecological risk indicator. In-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients is disproportionately concentrated in older, female, and indigenous populations, highlighting the need for targeted surveillance, equitable healthcare access and integrated One Health strategies to reduce the burden of HCPS in Chile.

Notifications were positively associated with higher male population rates and greater burned area due to forest fires, and negatively associated with urbanization and population density. Among 462 hospitalized patients, the in-hospital case-fatality ratio was 19.7%. Older age, female sex and indigenous group affiliation were significantly associated with higher in-hospital mortality risk among hospitalized patients. Shorter hospitalization duration and greater number of surgical interventions, as correlates of clinical severity and complexity, were also associated with in-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients. Conclusions: HCPS notification burden in Chile is shaped by environmental and demographic factors, with forest fire activity representing a novel and actionable ecological risk indicator. In-hospital mortality among hospitalized patients is disproportionately concentrated in older, female, and indigenous populations, highlighting the need for targeted surveillance, equitable healthcare access and integrated One Health strategies to reduce the burden of HCPS in Chile. papers.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in children: a systematic scoping review of presentation, critical care management, and outcomes.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome/hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) is rare but can progress rapidly from a nonspecific febrile prodrome to respiratory failure, shock, and multiorgan dysfunction. Pediatric-specific evidence is limited, and a comprehensive map of the clinical literature is lacking. METHODS: We conducted a systematic scoping review per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidance (protocol registered at DOI:10.17605/OSF.IO/MZDN4). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception to May 2026. Eligible reports described children or adolescents (age ≤18 years) with HCPS/HPS and extractable pediatric clinical data. Two reviewers independently screened records, assessed overlap, extracted data, and appraised reporting quality using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. RESULTS: Of 2208 database records, 20 reports were included in the core pediatric synthesis after removal of 976 duplicates and screening. Reports were concentrated in the Americas. Recurrent features included fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and shock. Severe cases required mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and in some cases renal replacement therapy. Larger pediatric case series and surveillance-level reports reported mortality of approximately 33% to 37%. Evidence was predominantly case-based with variable reporting completeness. CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric HCPS/HPS is rare but potentially rapidly fatal. Early suspicion in endemic regions or after rodent exposure, with prompt supportive critical care and timely consideration of advanced cardiopulmonary support, is central to management.

analysis.background: Pediatric hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome/hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) is rare but can progress rapidly from a nonspecific febrile prodrome to respiratory failure, shock, and multiorgan dysfunction.
analysis.main_directions: The review maps pediatric clinical literature, emphasizing presentation, critical‑care interventions (mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, ECMO, renal replacement) and mortality outcomes.
analysis.current_state: From 2,208 screened records, 20 reports (mainly from the Americas) were synthesized, revealing common features such as fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, pulmonary edema, and a mortality of roughly 33‑37 %.
analysis.gaps: Evidence is predominantly case‑based with variable reporting completeness, and pediatric‑specific data remain scarce, limiting robust epidemiologic or therapeutic conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Pediatric HCPS/HPS is rare but can progress rapidly to severe multiorgan failure. Main directions: The scoping review charts presentation, critical‑care interventions (ventilation, vasoactive drugs, ECMO, renal replacement) and outcomes. Current state: Twenty reports, chiefly from the Americas, show common signs (fever, GI symptoms, thrombocytopenia, pulmonary edema) and a mortality of ~33‑37 %. Gaps: Data are largely case‑based with inconsistent reporting, leaving pediatric evidence limited. Future research: Prospective multicenter studies with standardized reporting and evaluation of advanced support (e.g., ECMO) are required to clarify risk factors, optimal care, and long‑term sequelae.

analysis_zh.background: 儿科 汉坦病毒心肺综合征/汉坦病毒肺综合征(HCPS/HPS)罕见,但可从非特异性发热前驱期迅速进展至呼吸衰竭、休克和多器官功能障碍。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述绘制儿科临床文献图谱,重点阐述表现、重症监护干预(机械通气、血管活性药物支持、体外膜氧合(ECMO)、肾脏替代治疗)以及死亡率结果。

analysis_zh.future_research: 需要前瞻性多中心队列、标准化病例报告以及系统评估高级支持方式(如 ECMO),以明确儿童的风险因素、最佳管理和长期结局。

papers.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: challenges faced by clinicians.

source_records.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: challenges faced by clinicians.

papers.full_text: Managing hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in pediatric patients is highly challenging due to rapid clinical decline, diagnostic ambiguity, and the lack of targeted antiviral therapies. The article by Weerapong et al addresses these challenges in this issue of Baylor University Medical Center Proceedings.1 While the disease is rare in children, it carries a very high mortality rate of 30% to 50% if not managed aggressively. Because children possess unique physiological vulnerabilities, clinicians face several distinct obstacles when managing HCPS. Diagnostic dilemmas and misinterpretations stem from the nonspecific prodrome, which consists of flu-like symptoms including fever, headache, myalgia, and gastrointestinal issues such as vomiting or abdominal pain. These symptoms mirror common, benign childhood infections like influenza, gastroenteritis, or respiratory syncytial virus, thereby delaying clinical suspicion. Furthermore, obtaining a clear history of rodent exposure is difficult, as children may not notice or recall contact with deer mouse droppings while playing outdoors. Crucially, the shift from a benign viral prodrome to severe respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock occurs abruptly, often within hours. Diffuse pulmonary capillary leakage causes massive, bilateral pleural effusions and pulmonary edema. Unlike typical septic shock, HCPS causes profound myocardial depression marked by an abnormally low cardiac index and elevated systemic vascular resistance. The lack of targeted drug therapies restricts clinical options purely to supportive care. Aggressive fluid resuscitation to correct hypotension routinely worsens pulmonary edema and hypoxemia due to the underlying capillary leak. Consequently, managing low cardiac output requires early, carefully titrated inotropic therapy rather than massive volume expansion. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation serves as the primary rescue therapy for refractory shock, but its deployment requires specialized pediatric centers and carries significant risks of severe hemorrhage or limb ischemia. Ultimately, successful management hinges on maintaining a high index of suspicion when history suggests exposure, initiating early and aggressive treatment for shock and respiratory failure, and ensuring rapid transfer to high-acuity pediatric centers. — Jamil A. Abbasi, MD Baylor Scott & White All Saints Medical Center, Fort Worth, Texas, USA jamil.abbasi@bswhealth.org References - 1.Lilitwat W, Mahindrakar N, Bhandari P, et al. Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in children: a systematic scoping review of presentation, critical care management, and outcomes. Proc (Bayl Univ Med Cent). 2026;39(6):1118–1127. doi: 10.1080/08998280.2026.2698359. [DOI] [PubMed] [Google Scholar]

analysis.background: HCPS in children is a rare but severe disease with rapid clinical decline, diagnostic ambiguity, and no specific antiviral therapy, leading to high mortality.
analysis.methods: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: Mortality in pediatric HCPS is reported at 30%–50% (F2); the disease can shift abruptly from a flu‑like prodrome to severe respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock within hours (F7); no targeted drug therapies exist, limiting care to supportive measures (F10); extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is the primary rescue therapy for refractory shock (F13).
analysis.contribution: The article underscores the need for high clinical suspicion, early aggressive supportive care, and rapid transfer to specialized pediatric centers to improve outcomes (F14).
analysis.limitations: Only abstract and partial text are available; no primary data, study design, or systematic analysis are presented.

papers.title: Prevalence and Genetic Diversity of Zoonotic Leptospira and Hantavirus in Rodents, Lanxi City, 2023-2025.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Leptospirosis (caused by Leptospira, a bacterium) and hantavirus disease (caused by hantavirus, a virus) are important zoonoses with rodents as main reservoirs. In this study, we investigated the prevalence and genetic diversity of Leptospira and hantavirus in rodents from rural Lanxi City, Zhejiang Province. Rodents showed a higher Leptospira carriage rate than the national average. All hantavirus isolates were Seoul virus (SEOV) and displayed high genetic divergence from vaccine strains. Notably, a unique local phylogenetic cluster of Leptospira borgpetersenii was identified, indicating potential vaccine mismatch and local evolutionary divergence. METHODS: Samples were collected from April 2023 to August 2025, with intensive trapping from April to August annually in 2023-2024 and additional sampling in April 2025. Liver and kidney tissues were collected via aseptic dissection. Real-time fluorescent PCR was used to detect pathogen nucleic acids, and gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis were performed on positive samples. RESULTS: A total of 350 rodents were captured, with Rattus norvegicus (brown rat) as the dominant species (80.00%). The overall Leptospira carriage rate was 7.14% (25/350), with the highest rate in R. norvegicus (7.86%). The overall hantavirus carriage rate was 1.43% (5/350), distributed mainly in R. norvegicus and Rattus flavipectus (yellow-breasted rat). No coinfection with both pathogens was detected. Genetic analysis identified 12 Leptospira strains as Leptospira interrogans and 2 as L. borgpetersenii; the latter showed genetic differences from domestic and foreign strains, suggesting a potential evolutionary trend. The two hantavirus strains were both SEOV, closely related to domestic SEOV strains from 2021 but with only 86.08-86.81% nucleotide homology to vaccine strains (e.g., 80-39, Z37), indicating natural variation. CONCLUSIONS: Rodents in rural Lanxi have a relatively high Leptospira carriage rate, and hantavirus is dominated by the SEOV type. R. norvegicus is the main host of both pathogens. Targeted monitoring and prevention/control measures should be strengthened. Natural genetic variation suggests potential antigenic drift and reduced vaccine matching, which requires further serological validation. Attention should be paid to the impact of pathogen genetic variation on control efforts.

analysis.background: Leptospirosis (Leptospira) and hantavirus disease are important zoonoses with rodents as the main reservoirs (A1).
analysis.methods: Rodents were trapped in rural Lanxi City, Zhejiang Province from April 2023 to August 2025 (A2, A6); 350 rodents were captured, predominantly Rattus norvegicus (A9); liver and kidney tissues were collected aseptically (A7) and screened by real‑time fluorescent PCR, followed by gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of positive samples (A8).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Leptospirosis and hantavirus are key rodent‑borne zoonoses (A1). Methods: Rodents were trapped in rural Lanxi City, Zhejiang Province (Apr 2023‑Aug 2025), 350 captured (mostly R. norvegicus), tissues tested by real‑time PCR and sequencing (A2, A6‑A8). Results: Leptospira prevalence was 7.14% (25/350) exceeding national levels; hantavirus prevalence was 1.43% (5/350), all Seoul virus with 86.08‑86.81% similarity to vaccine strains, and a unique local L. borgpetersenii cluster was found; no co‑infections (A3‑A5, A9‑A16). Contribution: Provides surveillance of pathogen prevalence and genetic variation, indicating possible vaccine mismatch and informing control strategies (A4, A5, A20). Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed methods and broader context are not reported.

papers.title: The 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak: a renewed call for global zoonotic preparedness
papers.abstract: The 2026 cluster of Andes virus (ANDV) infection linked to the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius resulted in 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable), including three deaths, and required the monitoring of more than 650 contacts across more than 30 countries and territories before the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026. Available evidence suggests a single land-based zoonotic exposure before embarkation, followed by limited person-to-person transmission on board. Although WHO assessed the global risk as low throughout, the event exposed recurring weaknesses in zoonotic preparedness, including delayed clinical recognition in a remote setting, maritime outbreak protocols oriented toward other pathogens, and the burden of multinational contact tracing for an infection with an incubation period of up to 6 weeks. This editorial examines these lessons in light of earlier ANDV outbreaks and argues for closer integration of One Health surveillance, maritime health security, and the International Health Regulations in preparing for rare but high-consequence zoonoses.
papers.journal: International Journal of Surgery: Global Health

papers.abstract: Nghiên cứu hồi cứu này nhằm mô tả đặc điểm dịch tễ các trường hợp nhiễm Hantavirus ở người và xácđịnh tỷ lệ mẫu huyết thanh chuột dương tính với Hantavirus tại các địa điểm ghi nhận ca bệnh ở Thànhphố Hồ Chí Minh giai đoạn 2012–2014. Dữ liệu được thu thập từ hệ thống giám sát bệnh truyền nhiễm củaViện Pasteur Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh. Kết quả ghi nhận 6 ca nhiễm Hantavirus ở người, không có tử vong.Năm 2014 có số ca cao nhất với 3 ca (50,0%); nam giới chiếm 83,3% và phần lớn ca bệnh trên 30 tuổi.Tất cả đều tăng creatinine huyết thanh (173–671 μmol/L), trong đó 4 ca giảm tiểu cầu (11.000–58.000 tếbào/mm3); tất cả đều hồi phục sau điều trị. Chuột và chất thải chuột được ghi nhận tại nơi sinh sống của tấtcả bệnh nhân. Trong 309 mẫu huyết thanh chuột được xét nghiệm, có 88 mẫu dương tính với Hantavirus(28,5%); tỷ trọng mẫu dương tính cao nhất được ghi nhận ở chuột cống (Rattus norvegicus) (87,5%). Kếtquả cho thấy Hantavirus lưu hành trong quần thể chuột tại các địa điểm ghi nhận ca bệnh, tiềm ẩn nguycơ phơi nhiễm ở người trong môi trường đô thị. Cần tăng cường giám sát ca bệnh, năng lực xét nghiệmHantavirus và giám sát định kỳ trên chuột nhằm hỗ trợ phát hiện sớm và triển khai các biện pháp phòng,chống kịp thời.

analysis.background: The retrospective study aimed to describe the epidemiological characteristics of human hantavirus infections and to determine the seroprevalence of hantavirus in rodent samples from locations where cases occurred in Ho Chi Minh City during 2012–2014 (A1).
analysis.methods: Data were obtained from the Ho Chi Minh City Pasteur Institute infectious‑disease surveillance system (A2); rodent and rodent‑waste specimens were collected at patients’ residences and serum tested for hantavirus antibodies (A6).
analysis.results: Six human cases were recorded with no deaths; 50.0% occurred in 2014 (A3). Males comprised 83.3% of cases, most were >30 years old (A4). All showed elevated serum creatinine (173–671 µmol/L) and four had thrombocytopenia (11 000–58 000 cells/mm³) (A4); all recovered after treatment (A5). Of 309 rodent serum samples, 88 (28.5%) were hantavirus‑positive (A7), with the highest positivity in Rattus norvegicus (87.5%) (A8).
analysis.contribution: The results indicate hantavirus circulation in urban rodent populations and a potential exposure risk to humans, underscoring the need for strengthened case and rodent surveillance and timely preventive actions (A9, A10).
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The retrospective study described human hantavirus cases and rodent seroprevalence in Ho Chi Minh City (2012‑2014). Methods: Surveillance data were used and rodent samples from patients' homes were tested for antibodies. Results: Six human cases (no deaths) were identified, 83.3% male, >30 y, all with high creatinine and four with low platelets; all recovered. Among 309 rodents, 28.5% were seropositive, highest in Rattus norvegicus (87.5%). Contribution: Demonstrates urban rodent hantavirus circulation and human exposure risk, supporting enhanced surveillance and preventive measures. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 2012–2014年胡志明市汉坦病毒人类感染的流行病学特征及病例地点鼠类感染情况:系列报告

analysis_zh.background: 回顾性研究旨在描述人类汉坦病毒感染的流行病学特征,并确定2012–2014年胡志明市病例发生地点的鼠类样本中汉坦病毒的血清流行率 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 数据来源于胡志明市巴斯德研究所传染病监测系统 (A2);在患者居住地采集鼠类及鼠类废弃物标本,并对血清进行汉坦病毒抗体检测 (A6)。
analysis_zh.results: 记录了6例人类病例,未出现死亡;其中50.0%发生在2014年 (A3)。男性占病例的83.3%,大多数年龄>30岁 (A4)。全部病例血清肌酐升高(173–671 μmol/L),其中4例出现血小板减少(11 000–58 000 cells/mm3) (A4);经治疗全部痊愈 (A5)。在309例鼠血清样本中,88例(28.5%)为汉坦病毒阳性 (A7),其中大鼠(Rattus norvegicus)阳性率最高,达87.5% (A8)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 结果表明汉坦病毒在城市鼠群中循环,并对人类构成潜在暴露风险,强调需加强病例和鼠类监测以及及时的预防措施 (A9, A10)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on understanding reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they intersect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on under­ standing reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they inter­ sect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is estab­ lished. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, work­ load, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively. KEYWORDS Andes virus, hantavirus, occupational exposure, One Health, orthohantavirus, preparedness, rodent reservoir, surveillance 1 Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, three-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses in the family Hantaviridae, order Elliovirales. Rodent-associated orthohantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) across much of Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syn­ drome (HCPS) in the Americas (1–3). The transmission cycle brings clinical care into contact with wildlife ecology, occupational health, veterinary practice, and laboratory biosafety. The defining One Health feature of hantavirus epidemiology is that the maintenance cycle operates entirely outside health services. Reservoir abundance and species composition, food availability, rainfall, temperature, land use, agricultural practice, housing quality, waste man­ agement and human behavior together determine whether infected animals contaminate spaces that people use (1, 4, 5). Humans are usually exposed by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent urine, feces, or saliva, or through direct contact with contaminated material. Inam and Khan  10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 Frontiers in Veterinary Science 02 frontiersin.org Prevention therefore depends on recognizing and modifying ecologi­ cal and occupational interfaces before a patient reaches clinical care. A systematic review of land cover and land use found agricultural land use positively associated with human infection risk in China and Brazil and forest cover positively associated with incidence in Europe, while associations with built-up areas differed in direction between studies (6). Surveillance coverage differs markedly between regions. Some countries have paired human case reporting with reservoir monitor­ ing for decades, while others rely on a few serosurveys or small wild­ life studies, and some have no structured reservoir data at all (7–9). This makes country comparisons difficult: few reported cases may indicate genuinely low transmission, limited diagnostic access, missed cases, or simply insufficient surveillance. A meta-analysis of small mammals across Southeast Asia estimated a pooled hantavirus preva­ lence of 6.07% among 11,806 animals, with the highest estimates in Indonesia and Singapore, in a region where human diagnostic recog­ nition remains limited (8). Work in Cambodia detected orthohanta­ virus RNA in 3.3% of 750 rodents and IgG seropositivity in 10.0% of people sampled at the same sites, with the highest rodent infection rates at urban rather than rural interfaces (9). Attention to these questions has been renewed by the 2026 multi- country Andes virus (ANDV) event linked to an expedition cruise ship, which produced 13 cases and three deaths, contact tracing across more than 30 countries and territories, and a sequence of international notifications before it was declared over in July 2026 (10). The event does not indicate that hantaviruses have become more widespread. It illustrates how a rare zoonosis moving through a mobile and medi­ cally constrained exposure network can rapidly test diagnostic referral pathways and risk communication in settings without endemic transmission. Recent field surveys, systematic reviews, and outbreak reports from 2024 to 2026 have expanded the evidence base on host range, land use, geographic surveillance gaps, and international response (6–10). Yet descriptive One Health reviews seldom specify how a low- capacity setting should move from baseline sampling to an investiga­ tion, or when an enhanced response can safely be reduced (11, 12). This review brings together reservoir biology, exposure, diagnostics, and surveillance to propose explicit, locally adaptable decision steps. The framework is an operational hypothesis, not an established standard. 2 Scope and evidence framing 2.1 Review design and information sources This structured narrative review brings together evidence on hantavirus reservoirs, human exposure, diagnosis, and One Health surveillance. We searched literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar, reference lists, and reports from public health agencies. The searches were updated in August 2026. Studies published from 2000 onward received particular attention, while earlier work was retained when it remained founda­ tional to the biology or clinical picture. Searches combined “hantavirus” or “orthohantavirus” with terms for five related domains: reservoir hosts and ecology; occupa­ tional, veterinary and household exposure; serology, molecular diag­ nosis and genomic epidemiology; surveillance, land use and climate; and Andes virus outbreaks and contact management. Terms and combinations were adapted to each database and refined as the review developed. The purpose was to examine evidence relevant to practical surveillance decisions across different epidemiological settings. 2.2 Evidence eligibility and selection Studies were retained when they directly informed one or more areas addressed in this review, including reservoir ecology and host relationships, animal-to-human exposure, human epidemiology, vet­ erinary or occupational risk, diagnostic and genomic methods, envi­ ronmental and land-use influences, surveillance, and preparedness. For specific epidemiological or laboratory statements, we relied mainly on peer-reviewed primary research; systematic and narrative reviews were used to place individual findings in a broader context. We also used guidance and outbreak reports from WHO, CDC, ECDC, and similar public or animal health agencies when these sources provided operational information not available in journal articles. We generally excluded papers devoted only to treatment or molecular mechanisms with no clear relevance to exposure or One Health surveillance, duplicate or substantially overlapping reports, studies with too little methodological detail to interpret, conference abstracts, and non-authoritative web sources. 2.3 Evidence synthesis and framework development Priority was given to primary epidemiological, virological, reser­ voir, genomic, diagnostic and occupational studies, with systematic reviews and authoritative narrative reviews used for broader contex­ tual statements. The synthesis was organized around five recurring questions: which animals maintain infection, where human exposure occurs, which populations are most exposed, how infection can be reliably detected, and how animal, human and environmental infor­ mation can be combined into surveillance and prevention (11, 13, 14). Because the literature considered differed substantially in study design, host species, geographic setting, diagnostic method, surveil­ lance intensity, and reported outcomes, quantitative pooling was not considered appropriate. Findings were synthesized narratively across epidemiological settings, with particular attention to consistency, directness of evidence, methodological clarity, and operational rele­ vance. Greater interpretive weight was given to longitudinal surveil­ lance, well-characterized reservoir studies, linked human-animal investigations, molecularly confirmed outbreaks, and studies with clearly described sampling and diagnostic methods. The tiered sur­ veillance framework was developed from recurring operational needs identified across these evidence domains and should be interpreted as an evidence-informed proposal rather than a formally validated guideline. We considered five dimensions when interpreting a study: rele­ vance to the question; reliable identification of the host and infection; a clear sampling denominator, time frame, and assay; a longitudinal or linked human-animal design when needed to support an inference; and agreement or disagreement with findings from other settings. A serological result without supporting exposure or molecular data was not taken as evidence of current transmission. These considerations informed the narrative synthesis rather than a formal quality score. Table 1 illustrates the kinds of evidence and methodological con­ straints that shaped the proposed surveillance framework. Inam and Khan  10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 Frontiers in Veterinary Science 03 frontiersin.org 2.4 Terminology and interpretive principles Terminology is used deliberately throughout. Hantavirus refers to the group, while orthohantavirus is used where taxonomic precision is required. We distinguish reservoir hosts, in which infection is per­ sistent and largely asymptomatic, from incidental hosts, and we dis­ tinguish serological evidence of past exposure from molecular detection of viral RNA, reservoir infection from human exposure, and human exposure from confirmed disease. Antibody detection in a rodent or a person is not by itself evidence of current transmission, and a positive rodent does not establish human disease risk in the absence of a plausible exposure pathway. One interpretive principle applies throughout: absence of pub­ lished surveillance is not equivalent to absence of infection. Evidence- sparse settings are therefore discussed in terms of surveillance gaps and preparedness needs rather than assumed local transmission or assumed local safety. The distinction matters particularly for neglected zoonoses, where diagnostic capacity and small-mammal sampling tend to be concentrated in a small number of research centers. 3 Hantavirus biology and disease spectrum The genome comprises small (S), medium (M) and large (L) seg­ ments encoding the nucleocapsid protein, the Gn/Gc glycoprotein precursor and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively (15). Genetic diversity arises through mutation, reassortment, pro­ longed host association and occasional host-switching events (16, 17). Inam and Khan  10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 Frontiers in Veterinary Science 04 frontiersin.org Many hantaviruses show strong evolutionary association with particular rodent or small-mammal hosts, but the relationship is more dynamic than a strict one-virus-one-host model (16, 17). Field data increasingly support this. A survey of small-mammal communi­ ties in New Mexico detected Sin Nombre virus (SNV) in 27% of ani­ mals sampled and recovered infectious virus from tissues and feces of species other than the recognized primary reservoir, indicating that alternative and previously unrecognized reservoirs can both maintain and shed the virus (18). Surveillance designs that sample only the expected host species may therefore underestimate both prevalence and the range of species contributing to environmental contamination. Old World orthohantaviruses, including Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) and Puumala virus (PUUV), are associated primarily with HFRS. Severity ranges from the comparatively mild nephropathia epidemica associated with PUUV to hemorrhage, hypotension, and acute kidney injury (2, 3, 19). New World viruses, notably Sin Nombre virus (SNV) and Andes virus (ANDV), are associated predominantly with HCPS, which can progress rapidly to pulmonary edema and cardiovascular compro­ mise (1, 2). Reported case fatality depends on the virus, the case defi­ nition, ascertainment period, and access to critical care. SEOV infection may be mild and can be missed without appropriate test­ ing (20). Table 2 places representative virus-host relationships beside their human syndromes and exposure settings. Its host associations are illustrative and should not be used to rule out infection in other small mammals. Much of the tissue injury appears to reflect an abnormal host response, increased vascular permeability, and platelet and endothelial dysfunction rather than widespread direct viral cytolysis (19, 21, 22). Reservoir rodents, by contrast, generally remain outwardly healthy despite persistent infection, allowing them to maintain and shed virus over long periods (23). Person-to-person spread is uncommon for hantaviruses. ANDV is the important exception, with transmission documented after close, prolonged contact, so infection-control measures become relevant in a way they usually are not for other hantaviruses (2, 10). 4 Reservoir ecology and routes of animal-associated exposure Human-pathogenic hantaviruses are maintained mainly in rodents, although related lineages also occur in shrews, moles, and bats (16, 17). Host associations help define geographic distribution, but surveillance is often more informative when risk is considered by setting rather than host species alone. papers.title: Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family Hantaviridae , with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment ( n = 166), M segment ( n = 48), and S segment ( n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L ( R 2 = 0.069), M ( R 2 = 0.021), and S ( R 2 = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular-clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed, Rattus -associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa.

Keywords: African hantaviruses, Phylogenomics, Orthohantavirus, One Health, Virus-host co-divergence, Zoonotic surveillance Introduction Emerging zoonotic viruses, including hantaviruses, continue to pose significant threats to global public health [1,2]. Africa is recognized as a hotspot for pathogen emergence because of its exceptional biodiversity, rapid environmental change, and increasing human–wildlife interactions [3]. Although considerable attention has focused on high-profile viral haemorrhagic fevers such as Ebola virus disease and Lassa fever, the diversity, ecology, and evolutionary history of many other zoonotic viruses remain poorly understood. Among these neglected pathogens are hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae), which were historically regarded as rodent-borne viruses distributed predominantly across Europe, Asia, and the Americas [1].. However, increasing molecular surveillance over the past two decades has demonstrated that hantaviruses are also widely distributed throughout Africa and circulate in diverse mammalian hosts, revealing substantially broader evolutionary and ecological diversity than previously recognized [4,5]. Members of the family Hantaviridae are enveloped viruses with a tripartite, negative- sense, single-stranded RNA genome comprising the Small (S), Medium (M), and Large (L) segments, which encode the nucleocapsid protein, glycoprotein precursor, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively [6]. Hantaviruses were traditionally considered highly host-associated viruses that evolved predominantly in rodents through long-term virus–host associations [7,8]. However, the discovery of genetically divergent hantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats substantially expanded this paradigm and demonstrated that the evolutionary diversity of the family extends across multiple mammalian orders [5,9]. These discoveries are particularly relevant to Africa, which represents an important but underexplored reservoir of hantavirus diversity, harbouring diverse ecosystems and mammalian hosts that remain incompletely characterized [10,11]. The discovery of Sangassou virus in the African wood mouse (Hylomyscus simus) in Guinea provided the first molecular evidence of an indigenous African rodent- associated hantavirus and established that African rodents harbour evolutionarily distinct viral lineages [6,12]. Subsequent investigations expanded the known diversity through the identification of Tanganya virus and Bowe virus in Crocidura shrews in Guinea [9], Azagny virus in the West African pygmy shrew (Crocidura obscurior) in Côte d'Ivoire [13], and highly divergent hantaviruses in banana pipistrelle bats (Neoromicia nanus) from Côte d'Ivoire [14]. Rodent-, shrew-, and bat-associated hantaviruses have subsequently been reported from Gabon, Sierra Leone, Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, Egypt, Senegal, Benin, and, more recently, Mali, highlighting the substantial host and geographic diversity of African hantaviruses [15,16,17,18]. The increasing availability of viral genomic sequences has revealed pronounced host- associated and geographic structuring among African hantaviruses [19,20]. Previous phylogenetic investigations indicate that indigenous African hantaviruses comprise several deeply divergent evolutionary lineages associated with rodents, shrews, and bats, whereas Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV), primarily associated with commensal Rattus species, exhibits broader phylogenetic relationships with globally distributed lineages [17]. These observations suggest that African hantavirus diversity comprises geographically structured endemic lineages alongside widely distributed commensal- rodent-associated viruses. Nevertheless, the evolutionary relationships among these lineages and the extent to which host association and geographic structure are conserved across genomic segments remain incompletely resolved because most previous studies have focused on individual virus species, single genomic segments, or restricted geographic regions. Understanding the evolutionary ecology of African hantaviruses is increasingly important because ecological disturbance, urbanization, agricultural intensification, climate variability, and habitat fragmentation are altering wildlife communities and potentially increasing opportunities for zoonotic spillover [3]. Human infection occurs predominantly through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected reservoir hosts, and retrospective serological investigations have provided evidence of human exposure in several African countries [4,6]. However, hantavirus infections remain poorly recognized in routine clinical practice because their nonspecific manifestations overlap with those of malaria, typhoid fever, Lassa fever, leptospirosis, and other endemic febrile illnesses [21]. Consequently, the burden of hantavirus infection in Africa is likely underestimated, particularly in countries such as Nigeria, where hantavirus diversity and human infection remain poorly characterized. The recent 2026 Andes virus outbreak associated with the M/V Hondius cruise ship further demonstrates the potential for hantaviruses to generate cross-border public-health events requiring multinational surveillance, laboratory investigation, contact tracing, and coordinated international responses [22]. These observations emphasize the need to strengthen hantavirus surveillance within broader One Health frameworks for emerging zoonotic disease detection and preparedness. The segmented genome of hantaviruses provides an important basis for investigating whether evolutionary patterns are consistently represented across different genomic regions. Because the L, M, and S segments encode proteins with distinct biological functions, they may experience different evolutionary constraints, rates of sequence change, and selective pressures [23,24]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and contains relatively conserved regions that can provide phylogenetic information across divergent lineages, whereas the M segment encodes the viral glycoprotein precursor involved in virus–host cell interactions and may exhibit substantial sequence variation among viral lineages. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein and provides an additional functionally distinct marker for resolving evolutionary relationships. Consequently, phylogenies reconstructed from individual genomic segments may differ in their ability to resolve deep and shallow evolutionary relationships, including geographic and host-associated lineages [11,23,24]. In addition, comparison of segment-specific phylogenies enables assessment of whether viral lineages share a common evolutionary history. Strong topological concordance among segment phylogenies supports a broadly shared evolutionary history, whereas phylogenetic incongruence may reflect genetic reassortment or other segment-specific evolutionary processes [25,26]. Reassortment can occur following co-infection of a host with genetically distinct viruses and may generate discordant evolutionary histories among genomic segments [6,26]. Comparative analysis across all three genomic segments is therefore important for distinguishing robust host- and geographic-associated evolutionary patterns from signals specific to individual genomic regions. Despite the increasing discovery of genetically diverse hantaviruses in Africa, a continent-wide comparative framework integrating evolutionary relationships, host associations, geographic structure, and genomic congruence remains limited [11,17,27]. In particular, the extent to which host- and geographic-associated phylogenetic patterns are concordantly recovered across the L, M, and S genomic segments remains poorly characterized at the continental scale. Addressing these gaps is important for understanding the evolutionary organization of African hantavirus diversity and for identifying genomic and ecological priorities for One Health surveillance. In the present study, we performed a continent-wide comparative phylogenomic analysis of African hantaviruses using the L, M, and S genomic segments. We analysed 281 full-length and partial coding sequences from 13 African countries together with representative global reference sequences to characterize host- associated and geographic structuring and assess phylogenetic congruence among genomic segments. Pairwise tanglegram analyses were used to assess topological congruence among the L, M, and S phylogenies and identify discordant relationships potentially consistent with reassortment. By integrating multi-segment phylogenetic evidence with reservoir-host and geographic information, this study establishes a continent-wide framework for understanding the evolutionary structure of African hantaviruses and provides a foundation for future genomic surveillance, One Health preparedness, and global health security. Materials and Methods Sequence dataset A total of 281 hantavirus nucleotide sequences representing the three genomic segments were analyzed: 48 M-segment, 67 S-segment, and 166 L-segment sequences (Supplementary Table 1). All sequences from Africa (Egypt, Senegal, Benin, Mali, Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Sierra Leone, Gabon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and Madagascar) were retrieved from National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank and represent isolates collected between 2004 and 2024 with no isolates from 2025 together with selected reference strains from Asia, Europe, and the Americas to provide global phylogenetic context. Sequence alignment Nucleotide sequences for each genomic segment (L, M, and S) were aligned independently using MAFFT v7 [28] with the --auto algorithm and otherwise default parameters. Alignments were inspected and manually edited in AliView v1.01 [29] to ensure positional homology. Ambiguously aligned regions and sites with excessive gaps were removed prior to phylogenetic inference. Phylogenetic inference Maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenies for each segment were inferred using IQ- TREE v2.1.3 [30]. For each alignment the best-fit nucleotide substitution model was selected by ModelFinder [31] implemented within IQ-TREE. Node support was assessed with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates [32]. The ML trees files were exported in Newick format with branch lengths in substitutions/site and visualized in interactive Tree Of Life version 7.6 iTOL [33]. Assessment of temporal signal Temporal signal of each segment dataset was evaluated using Clockor2 v1.9.1 [34] (https://clockor2.github.io). ML trees with branch lengths in substitutions/site (Newick format) and sampling dates (from sequence metadata or CSV file) were used as inputs. Root-to-tip regression was performed independently for the L, M, and S datasets. The temporal signal was judged insufficient to support reliable molecular clock dating. Therefore, time-calibrated Bayesian phylogenetic analyses and molecular clock dating were not performed. Comparative phylogenetic analysis and detection of reassortment To ensure consistent taxon labels across segment datasets, isolates were assigned unique identifiers (HTV001–HTV198) and a mapping file linking identifiers to accession numbers and metadata is provided in Supplementary Table 1. Trees were rooted consistently by midpoint rooting in FigTree v1.4.4 [35]. Congruence among the L, M, and S genomic segments, ML trees were compared using Dendroscope v3.5.7 [36]. Pairwise tanglegrams (L–M, L–S, and M–S) were generated using the Tanglegram module; the built-in untangling algorithm was applied to minimize edge crossings while preserving topology. Trees used for tanglegrams were exported in NEXUS format. Putative reassortment events were identified by examining isolates that occupied incongruent phylogenetic positions between paired segment trees. Particular attention was given to taxa that clustered within different evolutionary lineages while maintaining strong branch support in the original phylogenetic analyses. Given that topological discordance may also arise from incomplete phylogenetic resolution, stochastic error, or differences in evolutionary histories among genomic segments, putative reassortment events were interpreted conservatively by integrating tanglegram patterns with branch support, host species, geographic origin, and the broader phylogenetic context. Results Dataset Characteristics We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the three hantavirus genomic segments: L, encoding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (n = 166), M, encoding the glycoprotein precursor (n = 48), and S, encoding the nucleocapsid protein (n = 67) (Supplementary Table 1). The dataset comprised sequences from 13 African countries spanning West n= 70, Central n=2, East n=46, and North Africa n= 16 and Madagascar n=91, together with representative global reference strains (supplementary table 1). African sequences were derived from diverse mammalian hosts, including rodents, shrews, and bats, allowing comparative assessment of host-associated and geographic phylogenetic structure. Assessment of Temporal Signal Root-to-tip regression showed weak temporal structure for the L, M and S datasets (R2 = 0.069, 0.021 and 0.046, respectively), indicating insufficient temporal signal for reliable molecular-clock inference. Consequently, time-calibrated phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses were not undertaken. Subsequent evolutionary comparisons were therefore based on phylogenetic topology, branch support, host association, and geographic distribution rather than divergence-time estimates. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment (n = 166), M segment (n = 48), and S segment (n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa. papers.title: Predictive Surveillance for Andes Virus Transmission in the Americas.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak linked to the M/V Hondius cruise ship exposed limitations in conventional, case-based surveillance for zoonotic threats with potential person-to-person transmission. In the present opinion and analysis article, the authors argue that predictive surveillance, supported by artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and the One Health approach, can strengthen preparedness for hantavirus transmission in the Americas. Current evidence suggests that selected models that incorporate epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent-related variables may provide an anticipatory window of 2 to 12 months, depending on context and data inputs. However, implementation requires more than technical capacity. It depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent model governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer to avoid widening inequities between health systems. Predictive surveillance should complement conventional surveillance by supporting risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public health action in areas where ecological and epidemiological signals converge.
papers.journal: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene

papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.
