papers.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. Importantly, responsibility for preventing emerging zoonoses should not rest exclusively with Ministries of Health but should be shared across the environmental, forestry and agricultural sectors [18]. Given the strong association between land-use change and zoonotic disease emergence, environmental policies should be regarded as an integral component of infectious disease prevention [14], [18]. Incorporating zoonotic disease risk into environmental impact assessments before large-scale deforestation, agricultural expansion or other ecosystem-altering activities could facilitate the identification of high-risk practices and inform mitigation strategies [18]. Likewise, strengthening surveillance programmes targeting wildlife reservoirs, particularly bats and rodents, together with advances in genomic surveillance, would improve the early detection of pathogens with zoonotic potential before widespread human transmission occurs [18]. Such proactive measures would shift the focus from responding to outbreaks toward preventing them by addressing their underlying anthropogenic drivers. As the recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks clearly demonstrate, the prevention of future pandemics depends not only on advances in medicine but also on the protection and sustainable management of the ecosystems upon which human health ultimately depends. Conclusion The recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks provide compelling evidence that anthropogenic environmental change is no longer a peripheral contributor to zoonotic disease emergence but one of its principal drivers. Deforestation, agricultural expansion and unsustainable land-use practices continue to reshape ecosystems, increase contact between humans and wildlife reservoirs, and facilitate pathogen spillover with potentially devastating public health consequences. As climate change and environmental degradation intensify, similar outbreaks are likely to become more frequent unless these upstream drivers are addressed. Future preparedness must therefore extend beyond improvements in diagnostics, therapeutics and outbreak surveillance to include policies that protect ecosystems, promote sustainable land management and integrate zoonotic disease risk into environmental decision-making. The One Health approach offers a scientifically grounded framework through which governments, public health authorities, environmental agencies and agricultural sectors can work collaboratively to mitigate the root causes of emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, preventing the next pandemic will depend not only on advances in medicine but also on our ability to recognize that safeguarding environmental integrity is inseparable from protecting human health. The question is no longer whether anthropogenic environmental change influences the emergence of zoonotic diseases, but whether global health policy will evolve rapidly enough to address these environmental drivers before the next pandemic emerges. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

KEYWORDS acute pancreatitis, case report, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, Seoul orthohantavirus Introduction Case presentation and clinical data A 33-year-old man presented with one week of recurrent fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He had no history of gallstones, hypertriglyceridemia, alcohol abuse, or other recognized risk factors for acute pancreatitis. Although viral gastroenteritis could explain fever, vomiting and watery diarrhea, the presence of epigastric tenderness on TYPE Case Report PUBLISHED 28 October 2026 DOI 10.3389/fmed.2026.1995402 Frontiers in Medicine 01 frontiersin.org physical examination together with marked peripancreatic- perirenal exudates identified on initial abdominal CT raised strong clinical suspicion for severe acute pancreatitis. Initial non-contrast abdominal CT showed peripancreatic and perirenal haziness, renal fascial thickening, and small-volume abdominopelvic effusion with mild pancreatic swelling, findings highly suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis (Figure 1). Initial supportive measures for suspected acute pancreatitis were implemented, including intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, octreotide infusion, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, and volume resuscitation. Of note, severe thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 109/L) was already documented on admission rather than developing during hospitalization. However, the patient demonstrated progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without biochemical elevation of pancreatic enzymes. Two abdominal CT examinations were performed: a non- contrast CT on hospital day 1 (admission), followed by contrast- enhanced abdominal CT on hospital day 2. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed progressive retroperitoneal exudation accompanied by newly developed bilateral pleural effusion and splenomegaly. Routine work-up for undifferentiated fever was sent before mNGS testing, including bacterial blood cultures, stool culture, and a respiratory-borne viral screening panel, all of which returned negative results. Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) laboratory screening was not performed because clinical suspicion for TMA was low: the patient lacked schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, had no severe neurologic manifestations, and mNGS rapidly identified Seoul orthohantavirus as the causative pathogen. Whole-blood mNGS detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus (HBV) and no bacterial or fungal pathogens. Hepatoprotective therapy consisted of intravenous reduced glutathione and magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate. Due to persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and unstable clinical status precluding oral feeding, the patient was kept nil per os (NPO) at admission, not as a standard mandatory intervention for suspected acute pancreatitis. Enteral nutrition was gradually initiated once abdominal symptoms improved. After supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, albumin supplementation, hepatoprotective therapy, and electrolyte correction, the patient recovered fully; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology (Figure 2). Laboratory and imaging findings Initial laboratory investigations showed a mixed acid-base disturbance, characterized by respiratory alkalosis with normal anion-gap (AnGap 2-10 mmol/L),hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and liver function injury. The most striking abnormality was profound thrombocytopenia (29 × 109/L); urinalysis revealed hematuria and proteinuria. Table 2 was revised to add serum amylase, lipase, serum triglyceride, serum urea, serum creatinine, sodium, potassium, hemoglobin values. Reticulocyte count was not tested in clinical practice; hemoglobin levels over serial time-points are presented to evaluate for bone-marrow suppression. Urine sediment examination did not demonstrate granular or hyaline casts. Serial urine output was prospectively recorded as part of intensive care monitoring; overall urine output remained adequate throughout hospitalization without anuria or oliguric renal failure. Mild anemia was observed (minimum hemoglobin 127 g/L). Serial changes in leukocytes, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages, transaminases, platelets, albumin, and coagulation parameters are summarized in Table 2. The dynamic clinical, laboratory, imaging, and management course across hospitalization is summarized in the diagnostic timeline (Table 1). Hospital course and management The initial working diagnosis was suspected severe acute pancreatitis, and management comprised nil-per-os status due to patient intolerance of oral intake, octreotide infusion, a proton- pump inhibitor, empirical antimicrobial therapy, and fluid resuscitation. When the severe thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction could not be explained by primary pancreatitis, HFRS was considered. On hospital day 3, whole-blood mNGS returned high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, confirming the diagnosis. Treatment was adjusted to include intravenous immunoglobulin, human albumin, hepatoprotective therapy, and electrolyte correction. Abdominal pain resolved, and platelet count, liver, and renal parameters gradually normalized. The patient was discharged on hospital day 11 in good clinical condition, with outpatient follow-up scheduled for monitoring of liver function and HBV. Discussion This case highlights a diagnostically challenging presentation in which Seoul orthohantavirus infection clinically and radiologically mimicked severe acute pancreatitis, underscoring the need to consider HFRS in the differential diagnosis of unexplained pancreatitis-like presentations (1). Acute pancreatitis is a recognized but rare complication of HFRS (2, 6), and its distinction from hantavirus-induced pancreatic involvement is notoriously difficult because of overlapping clinical and imaging features (9). The present case further illustrates that peripancreatic exudation and retroperitoneal fluid —hallmark findings of severe acute pancreatitis—can also result from the profound systemic capillary leakage and retroperitoneal edema characteristic of hantavirus infection (4, 5). In this context, marked thrombocytopenia, renal impairment with hematuria and proteinuria, and the absence of typical pancreatitis risk factors constituted pivotal clues that prompted consideration of an alternative etiology (9). Moreover, the normal pancreatic enzyme levels observed here demonstrate that Abbreviations HFRS, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; AP, acute pancreatitis; SAP, severe acute pancreatitis; CT, computed tomography; mNGS, metagenomic next-generation sequencing; HBV, hepatitis B virus; hsCRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase; IVIG, intravenous immunoglobulin; PLT, platelet count; DIC, disseminated intravascular coagulation. Liu and Song 10.3389/fmed.2026.1995402 Frontiers in Medicine 02 frontiersin.org biochemical markers alone cannot reliably exclude HFRS in suspected pancreatitis (10). It should be acknowledged that severe acute pancreatitis itself may produce thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction secondary to systemic inflammation. However, several features argued against primary acute pancreatitis in this patient: thrombocytopenia was already present at initial presentation as a critical-value finding before any expected inflammatory peak of pancreatitis; renal injury was accompanied by prominent urinary findings (hematuria and proteinuria) typical for hantavirus-mediated tubular injury rather than purely pre-renal renal impairment secondary to pancreatitis-related hypovolemia; and serum amylase/lipase remained within normal reference ranges throughout admission despite extensive peripancreatic exudates on CT imaging. (A, C) Non-contrast abdominal CT acquired on hospital day 1 (admission). White arrows indicate the pancreas, peripancreatic fat- stranding inflammatory exudates, and thickened bilateral prerenal fascia with perirenal exudates. These radiological features initially raised high clinical suspicion for severe acute pancreatitis. (B, D) Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT acquired on hospital day 2. After contrast administration, the pancreatic parenchyma shows no definite necrosis or large-scale parenchymal destruction. White arrows mark the pancreatic gland. However, extensive retroperitoneal involvement with a relatively preserved pancreatic gland reflects the underlying pathophysiological hallmark of hantavirus infection —virus-induced increased microvascular permeability leading to fluid extravasation into the retroperitoneal space. Prior case reports of HFRS mimicking acute pancreatitis have generally relied on single- time-point scans and could not capture this evolving radiological signature (7). Recognition of this distinctive pattern is of substantial practical importance, particularly in endemic regions (14, 15). From a clinical standpoint, progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic changes on follow-up CT, when accompanied by thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction, should prompt clinicians to broaden the differential beyond pancreatic pathology. analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by orthohantaviruses can present atypically, closely mimicking acute pancreatitis and posing significant diagnostic challenges.
analysis.methods: This case report describes a 33-year-old man with fever, vomiting, and diarrhea; diagnosis was confirmed via whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) and dynamic CT imaging.
analysis.results: mNGS detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus and concurrent hepatitis B virus; the patient exhibited profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10^9/L), renal impairment, and retroperitoneal exudation without elevated pancreatic enzymes, and recovered fully with supportive care.
analysis.contribution: The case highlights that disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key clues to distinguish Seoul orthohantavirus infection from severe acute pancreatitis, with mNGS enabling early pathogen confirmation.
analysis.limitations: As a single case report, findings are not generalizable; the evidence is limited to the abstract and partial full text, and specific epidemiological exposure history is not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by orthohantaviruses can mimic acute pancreatitis, creating diagnostic difficulties. Methods: This case report details a 33-year-old man with fever and gastrointestinal symptoms, diagnosed using dynamic CT and whole-blood mNGS. Results: mNGS identified high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus and concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient presented with profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10^9/L), renal impairment, and retroperitoneal exudation, but lacked elevated pancreatic enzymes. He recovered fully with supportive care and intravenous immunoglobulin. Contribution: The study identifies disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and preserved pancreatic parenchyma as key diagnostic clues, demonstrating mNGS's utility in early pathogen confirmation. Limitations: The evidence is derived from a single case report and partial text, limiting generalizability; specific exposure history is not reported.

papers.title_zh: 病例报告:由首尔 正汉坦病毒 引起的 肾综合征出血热,模拟重症急性胰腺炎:动态影像演变及通过mNGS确认病原

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)由 正汉坦病毒es 引起,可表现为非典型,极其类似急性胰腺炎,带来显著的诊断挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 本病例报告描述了一名33岁男性,出现发热、呕吐和腹泻;诊断通过全血宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)和动态CT影像确认。
analysis_zh.results: mNGS检测到高拷贝首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 及同步的乙型肝炎病毒;患者出现严重血小板减少(最低值 29 × 10^9/L)、肾功能受损和腹膜后渗出,胰酶未升高,经过支持治疗后完全康复。

papers.title: Integrated in Silico Method for Virtual Screening and Interaction Profiling of Repurposed and Natural Inhibitor Candidates Against the Rdrp of the Newly Reported ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026 Orthohantavirus
papers.abstract: Introduction: The rapid release of complete viral genome sequences enables early computational prioritization of antiviral candidates before experimental screening becomes available. Objectives: This study evaluated the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp; L protein) of the newly reported ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026 orthohantavirus as an antiviral drug-design target. Methods: The L-segment-derived RdRp sequence was obtained from the public Virological.org report, modeled with AlphaFold, inspected against the NCBI Conserved Domain Database, and submitted to CB-Dock2 for binding-cavity prediction. The predicted pocket (X = 5.872, Y = 29.895, Z = -5.566) was used for DrugRep screening of 100 FDA-approved/repurposed and 100 natural TCMML compounds, which were then independently rescored with KDeep. Results: In the repurposed library, DB00511 and DB11581 gave the strongest DrugRep scores (-10.2), whereas DB00864 gave the highest KDeep pIC50 (7.1249); consensus ranking prioritized DB00511, DB00390 and DB01396. In the natural-product library, T0295 scored best with DrugRep (-9.8) and T8166 with KDeep (7.3537); consensus ranking prioritized T8166, T0295, T6473 and T3809. Interaction analysis supported these candidates through recurrent hydrogen-bond and hydrophobic contacts, including GLU129, SER157, THR170, ALA1463, TRP1464, ARG1544 and GLU1545. Conclusions: The combined DrugRep-KDeep-interaction workflow provides a rational computational shortlist for downstream redocking, molecular dynamics, ADMET profiling and experimental prioritization.

papers.title: A Case Report of Hantavirus Capillary Leak Syndrome in the Southwestern United States.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but frequently fatal viral disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Early symptoms are nonspecific, but the disease can rapidly progress to severe respiratory compromise and shock due to profound capillary leak. We report the case of a previously healthy 20-year-old man who initially presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and progressive weakness after occupational exposure on a ranch in southwestern Arizona. He quickly developed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), septic shock, and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The initial infectious workup was negative. His clinical course was complicated by respiratory failure requiring intubation and vasopressor support. Computed tomography of his chest showed pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions despite aggressive diuresis, requiring bilateral chest tubes. He gradually improved with supportive care, was successfully extubated, weaned off oxygen, and discharged home with outpatient rehabilitation. His diagnosis was later confirmed with a serum ELISA test which was positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of HCPS, particularly when gastrointestinal symptoms predominate early in the illness. In endemic areas with rodent exposure history, hemoconcentration and thrombocytopenia, along with signs of volume overload and rapidly progressive acute respiratory failure, should raise suspicion for hantavirus infection. Identification and supportive care are the mainstay of treatment. Although this patient did not require ECMO, transfer to an ECMO center may be beneficial to support recovery during the cardiopulmonary phase, as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS is a rare but often fatal disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted via aerosolized rodent excreta. Methods: A 20‑year‑old man from southwestern Arizona with rodent exposure was diagnosed by hantavirus IgM/IgG ELISA. Results: He developed hemoconcentration (Hct 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000/µL), septic shock, non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema, required intubation, vasopressors, and chest tubes, but recovered with supportive care and was discharged. Contribution: The report underscores diagnostic complexity when GI symptoms dominate and advises early suspicion of HCPS in endemic settings with these laboratory and clinical signs. Limitations: Only abstract information is available and the report describes a single case, limiting generalizability.

papers.title_zh: 关于美国西南部汉坦病毒毛细血管漏综合征的病例报告。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)是一种罕见但常致命的病毒性疾病,流行于美洲,主要通过吸入鼠类排泄物的气溶胶传播。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者描述了一名来自亚利桑那州西南部、20岁的男性,职业接触啮齿动物;诊断随后通过血清ELISA检测 汉坦病毒 IgM 和 IgG 阳性得到确认。
analysis_zh.results: 患者迅速出现血液浓缩(血细胞比容 58%)、血小板减少(17,000 细胞/μL)、败血性休克、非心源性肺水肿,需要插管、血管加压药支持,并因大面积胸腔积液置入双侧胸管,但在支持治疗下逐渐好转,出院回家。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该病例凸显了当胃肠症状为主时的诊断复杂性,并强调在流行地区,血液浓缩、血小板减少和快速呼吸衰竭应提高对 汉坦病毒 感染的警觉。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要数据,且结果来源于单一患者,限制了更广泛的推断。

papers.title: Hantavirus on a Cruise Ship: What COVID-19 Taught Us.
papers.abstract: Delayed recognition of the mechanics of aerosol transmission-the primary mode of spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)-at the beginning of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic led to inadequate early recommendations regarding nonpharmaceutical interventions and poor initial messaging about how to reduce infection risk. We highlight key epidemiological details of Andes virus (ANDV) transmission on the MV Hondius cruise ship and during prior reported outbreaks with confirmed person-to-person spread in Argentina, which, together, suggest aerosol spread may be a key mechanism of transmission of ANDV between source cases and susceptible contacts in permissible environmental settings.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

analysis.background: Delayed recognition of aerosol transmission of SARS‑CoV‑2 at the start of the COVID‑19 pandemic highlighted gaps in understanding aerosol spread for other pathogens, prompting investigation of Andes virus (ANDV).
analysis.methods: The authors reviewed key epidemiological details of ANDV transmission on the MV Hondius cruise ship and prior Argentine outbreaks with confirmed person‑to‑person spread.
analysis.results: The review suggests that aerosol spread may be a key mechanism of ANDV transmission between source cases and susceptible contacts in permissive environmental settings.
analysis.contribution: Identifies aerosol transmission as a plausible route for ANDV, informing surveillance and infection‑control strategies on cruise ships and similar environments.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available; detailed data, sample sizes, quantitative results, and methodological specifics are not reported.

papers.title: Hantavirus: An Emerging Global Zoonotic Threat—From Molecular Basis to Clinical Management and Public Health Perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonotic viral disease caused by hantaviruses of the family Hantaviridae, primarily transmitted to humans through exposure to infected rodent urine, feces, saliva, or contaminated aerosols. The disease presents mainly in two clinical forms: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), prevalent in Asia and Europe, and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS)/Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas. The historical recognition of hantavirus began during the Korean War (1950–1953), when thousands of soldiers developed Korean hemorrhagic fever. In 1978, Ho-Wang Lee isolated the Hantaan virus from Apodemus agrarius, marking a major scientific breakthrough. Subsequent decades witnessed the identification of multiple hantavirus species, including Seoul, Puumala, Dobrava-Belgrade, Sin Nombre, and Andes viruses, each associated with distinct rodent reservoirs and clinical manifestations. A major epidemiological milestone occurred in 1993 with the outbreak of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome in the Four Corners region of the United States, leading to the discovery of Sin Nombre virus. Increasing urbanization, climate change, deforestation, and closer human–rodent interactions have contributed to the global emergence of hantavirus infections in the 21st century. Advances in molecular diagnostics, including reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and serological testing, have enhanced disease surveillance and early diagnosis. This review highlights the historical evolution, epidemiology, transmission, and growing public health significance of hantavirus infection worldwide. Keywords: Hantavirus infection; Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS); Hantavirus Pulmonary

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒感染是一种新发的动物源性病毒性疾病,通过接触受感染的啮齿动物尿液、粪便、唾液或受污染的气溶胶传播给人类 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 在提供的证据中未报告。
analysis_zh.results: 该疾病首次在朝鲜战争期间被确认 (A3);汉滩病毒于1978年从田野鼠(Apodemus agrarius)中分离得到 (A4);随后鉴定出多种汉坦病毒种类(首尔病毒、普马拉病毒、Dobrava‐Belgrade、Sin Nombre、安第斯病毒),与不同的啮齿动物宿主相关 (A5);1993年美国四角地区的汉坦病毒肺综合征(HPS)暴发导致发现Sin Nombre病毒 (A6)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本综述综合了汉坦病毒感染在全球范围内的历史演变、流行病学、传播途径以及日益增长的公共卫生意义 (A9)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细方法、定量数据和原始研究结果。

papers.title: Evaluation of Andes virus vaccine-derived human antibody for protection in Syrian hamsters: a passive transfer study using phase 1 trial sera.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and is uniquely capable of person-to-person transmission, with no licenced vaccines or therapeutics available. A Phase 1 trial (NCT03682107) demonstrated that an ANDV DNA vaccine targeting Gn/Gc envelope proteins elicits neutralising antibodies in humans. We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model. METHODS: Day 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). Neutralising antibody levels were quantified using pseudovirion neutralisation assays (PsVNA) and plaque reduction neutralisation tests (PRNT) to determine exploratory cutoff titres predicting survival. FINDINGS: Human antibodies from DNA-vaccinated subjects-unlike normal IgG-conferred significant protection against lethal ANDV challenge in both experiments. The exploratory cutoff titres predicting protection were determined to be 31-184 for PsVNA50 and 20-80 for PRNT50, depending on the analysis population and model parameters. INTERPRETATION: Vaccine-induced human antibodies are sufficient to protect against lethal ANDV infection in an established animal model. If confirmed, these results indicate that neutralising antibody titres could serve as a surrogate endpoint and correlate of protection for future hantavirus Gn/Gc-targeted vaccines. FUNDING: Defense Health Program and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

papers.title: Dual-Target Inhibition of Puumala Virus Entry Glycoproteins Gn and Gc by Moringa oleifera -Derived Phytochemicals: An Integrated Computational Study
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), a member of the Orthohantavirus genus, causes nephropathia epidemica, an intermediate type of hemorrhagic fever with renal dysfunction, yet no approved antiviral therapy is currently available. Viral entry is initiated by the coordinated actions of the attachment glycoprotein Gn and fusion glycoprotein Gc, making simultaneous inhibition of these proteins an attractive antiviral strategy. Here, we employed a combined computational workflow to identify dual-target inhibitors of PUUV entry glycoproteins from Moringa oleifera phytochemicals. 72 phytochemicals were retrieved and docked by molecular docking to identify high-affinity binders, while he top-ranked compounds were subsequently evaluated for drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic behavior, toxicity, and predicted biological activities to assess their therapeutic suitability. Complex stability and binding mechanisms were further investigated through 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) and MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations. Quercetin and kaempferol showed the lowest binding energies toward Gn (−9.8 and −9.7 kcal/mol) and Gc (−10.4 and −10.0 kcal/mol), respectively. Both phytochemicals demonstrated favorable drug-like properties, high gastrointestinal absorption, no predicted toxicity, and positive bioactivity scores. MDS confirmed stable protein–ligand complexes with minimal structural fluctuations, and MM-GBSA analysis further validated strong binding, with quercetin exhibiting the most favorable binding free energies against Gn (−84.24 kcal/mol) and Gc (−98.45 kcal/mol). These findings identify quercetin and kaempferol as promising dual-target inhibitors that may simultaneously disrupt PUUV attachment and membrane fusion, warranting further experimental validation.

Complex stability and binding mechanisms were further investigated through 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) and MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations. Quercetin and kaempferol showed the lowest binding energies toward Gn (−9.8 and −9.7 kcal/mol) and Gc (−10.4 and −10.0 kcal/mol), respectively. Both phytochemicals demonstrated favorable drug-like properties, high gastrointestinal absorption, no predicted toxicity, and positive bioactivity scores. MDS confirmed stable protein–ligand complexes with minimal structural fluctuations, and MM-GBSA analysis further validated strong binding, with quercetin exhibiting the most favorable binding free energies against Gn (−84.24 kcal/mol) and Gc (−98.45 kcal/mol). These findings identify quercetin and kaempferol as promising dual-target inhibitors that may simultaneously disrupt PUUV attachment and membrane fusion, warranting further experimental validation.

analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用计算工作流,检索了72种辣木(Moringa oleifera)植物化学成分,进行分子对接以识别高亲和力结合物,并对排名靠前的化合物进行药物相似性、药代动力学、毒性和生物活性评估;随后通过100纳秒分子动力学模拟和MM‐GBSA结合自由能计算进一步评估其稳定性和结合机制。
